title: Governments must protect conscience but never control it
setting: A general assembly of Church members met in Kirtland, Ohio, on 17 August 1835 and accepted the first edition of the Doctrine and Covenants. Oliver Cowdery and William W. Phelps then presented this declaration, and the assembly voted to print it in the book. Joseph Smith was away in Michigan Territory, and the author is uncertain; Cowdery may have written most of it. The Saints’ 1833 expulsion from Jackson County, Missouri, was a main reason for it. The JSP links the last paragraph to Missouri charges that the Church favored abolition.
summary: This is a declaration of belief, not a revelation; each paragraph begins “We believe”. It says God instituted governments and holds people accountable for how they make and run laws. Good laws must protect conscience, property, and life. People must sustain the governments that protect their rights, and sedition is condemned. Civil officers should punish crime but never control conscience, and no religion should be favored by the state. Churches may discipline members only by removing fellowship, never by taking property or life. People should appeal to the law for wrongs, but may defend themselves when the law cannot act in time. The last paragraph says preaching to enslaved people against their masters’ wishes is unlawful and dangerous.

contextNote.title: Freedom of conscience as the test of a government
contextNote.text: The Saints had just lost homes and land in Jackson County without protection from the state. Verse 4 answers a basic question: how far may government reach into religion? It says the magistrate “should restrain crime, but never control conscience”. Verse 2 gives the reason: no government keeps peace unless it secures “the free exercise of conscience”. Verse 9 adds the other side, rejecting any union of one church with civil power. In this passage, conscience means a person’s religious belief and worship, answerable to God alone.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 133–134 uses this declaration to teach that governments should protect the freedom to worship. How do verses 4 and 9 balance obeying the law with keeping religion free from state control?

jsp.title: Appendix 4: Declaration on Government and Law, circa August 1835 [D&C 134]

reviewNote: Read all 12 verses. Official heading gives the 17 August 1835 Kirtland general assembly and the preamble's purpose. JSP historical introduction read: authorship unclear, Oliver Cowdery possibly primary author, Joseph Smith absent in Michigan until 23 August and later endorsed it (April 1836 letter); Jackson County expulsion as main motive; verse 12 linked to the Church's wish to counter charges of abolitionism in Missouri. Sidney Rigdon is included because he presented the book at the assembly, not because the text names him. Verse 12 on enslaved people summarized factually without comment. Fact-check 2026-10-12: setting gave no context for verse 12 on enslaved people; added the JSP’s note that it answered Missouri charges of abolitionism, for balance.
